extra.message: console.log in a production path. It bypasses the logger's redaction, its levels and its destination — a line here is unstructured, unfiltered and un-turn-off-able.

Request data reaches a log call unencoded (CWE-117). A newline in that value forges a log line, which is how an attacker writes "authentication succeeded" into the file an incident is later reconstructed from.

Request data reaches a log call unencoded (CWE-117). A newline in that value forges a log line, which is how an attacker writes "authentication succeeded" into the file an incident is later reconstructed from.

A secret-shaped field passed to a log call. Logs outlive the request, sit outside the product's access control, and get shipped to third-party aggregators — a token that reaches one is a token to rotate.

Logged and rethrown. The caller will log it again, and the incident timeline gets the same failure three times at three levels of the stack — log it where it is handled, or rethrow it where it is not.
Step-numbered narration. Three of these in a row usually means the code was written to a plan and the plan was left behind as comments; the structure they describe should be functions with names.

try/catch inside a loop body. Sometimes deliberate (continue past one bad row), often a swallowed failure repeated N times with nobody counting. If it is deliberate, the catch should record how many it skipped.

An empty or comment-only catch block. The failure still happened; the only thing removed was anyone's chance of knowing. If the error genuinely does not matter, say so by handling it — a logged line, a fallback with a comment explaining why it is safe.

A catch block that returns an empty value. The caller cannot tell "there is nothing" from "we failed to find out", and those are different facts — this is the shape behind most "the dashboard shows zero" bugs.
A function that exists and does nothing but refuse. Exported stubs read as capabilities from the outside — a caller sees the name, not the throw — which is how "we support that" survives into a demo.

A comment restating what the next line does. It costs a line to read and goes stale the moment the code changes — a comment earns its place by saying WHY, or by naming a constraint the code cannot express.

An emoji in a comment. Harmless once; at scale it is the clearest tell of generated commentary nobody edited, and it does not survive a grep, a terminal without a font, or a diff someone reads at 6am.

Filler phrasing in a comment. "It is important to note that" and its relatives carry no information — they are the written equivalent of clearing your throat, and they are what a model produces when it has nothing specific to say.
